title: Gun-wielding man wanted police to fire, inquest told
article: A coroner's jury has been asked to find that Henry Masuka, who died in a hail of police gunfire on Jan. 1, 2000, in a downtown Toronto hospital, committed "suicide by cop."

The term refers to a growing but little-understood phenomenon of people who want to die and goad police officers into killing them. Unable or unwilling to kill themselves, these suicidal people create a confrontation with police that will likely result in their own death.

Lawyer Gary Clewley, who represents the officers who killed the 26-year-old father of four just minutes into the year 2000, said Mr. Masuka's actions that night indicate he wanted to die. "The only logical conclusion is suicide," Mr. Clewley told the jury in his closing submission yesterday.
Bob Ash, the coroner's counsel, also leaned toward a suicide finding, although he told the jury they could also find a verdict of homicide.
Both lawyers outlined some of the signs of a suicide attempt the night Mr. Masuka held a gun on Dr. Richard Yu, an emergency-room physician at St. Michael's Hospital.

Mr. Masuka had taken his three-month-old son there because he said the boy had difficulty breathing. He pulled the gun, which later turned out to be an unloaded pellet gun, when hospital staff didn't immediately look after his baby, who later was found to have a simple cold.

The signs, the lawyers said, were clear: Mr. Masuka set a midnight deadline, saying it would all be over by then; he taunted police, saying, "Shoot me. Shoot me," as he pointed to his chest; he asked hospital staff to call a television station; he was outnumbered and couldn't expect to escape the seven submachine guns pointed at him; he suddenly announced he wanted to sing to his son, then said, "I'm going to end this right now," and leaned over his hostage.
At that precise moment, two officers shot Mr. Masuka in the head.
"The deliberate movement toward Dr. Yu was designed to get police to shoot," Mr. Clewly said.
Peter Rosenthal, who acted for the Masuka family at the inquest, dismissed the suicide theory, saying the death was a homicide. Such a finding carries no legal consequences at inquests.
